notes.h: Why structural analysis matters in aircraft design
notes.body:
A first course in aircraft structures usually starts by placing structural analysis inside the wider design process. An aircraft structure must carry its loads safely, stay stiff enough to work properly, and be as light as possible, because every kilogram of structure is a kilogram of payload or fuel lost.

What the structure must do
- Strength: carry the design loads without breaking or yielding.
- Stiffness: limit deflections (for example, wing bending and twist affect aerodynamics and can cause aeroelastic problems such as flutter or divergence).
- Stability: thin members and panels must not buckle under compression or shear.
- Durability: resist fatigue crack growth and corrosion over the service life.

Loads and safety factors
- Limit load: the largest load expected in service (from manoeuvres, gusts, landing, pressurisation).
- Ultimate load = limit load × factor of safety. For civil transport aircraft certified to EASA CS-25 or FAA Part 25, the standard factor of safety is 1.5.
- The structure must carry limit load without detrimental permanent deformation, and ultimate load without failure (for at least 3 seconds under the certification rules for large aeroplanes).

The three pillars of every analysis
Every problem in this pack is solved with the same three ingredients:
- Equilibrium: forces and moments balance (ΣF = 0, ΣM = 0) for the whole body and for any part cut from it.
- Compatibility: the deformations fit together; members that are joined move together and supports impose known displacements.
- Constitutive law: how the material relates stress to strain (here, linear elasticity, σ = Eε).
If equilibrium alone gives all the internal forces, the structure is statically determinate. If not, it is statically indeterminate (redundant), and compatibility plus the constitutive law are needed as well.

Idealisation
Real structures are modelled as simpler ones: pin-jointed frameworks (members carry axial force only), beams (carry bending and shear), shafts (carry torque) and thin-walled sections (skin–stringer wing boxes and fuselages). Choosing a sensible idealisation and drawing a correct free-body diagram are the first marks in almost every exam question.

Material choice: specific properties
Because weight matters, materials are compared using specific properties:
- Specific stiffness E/ρ: aluminium alloy (≈ 70 GPa, 2700 kg/m³) ≈ 26 MJ/kg; steel (≈ 200 GPa, 7850 kg/m³) ≈ 25 MJ/kg; titanium (≈ 110 GPa, 4500 kg/m³) ≈ 24 MJ/kg.
- The common metals have similar E/ρ, which is why carbon-fibre composites (much higher E/ρ in the fibre direction) are attractive.
- Specific strength σ_y/ρ matters for strength-critical parts.

Exam tips: state your idealisation and assumptions, draw the free-body diagram first, and say explicitly which of equilibrium, compatibility and the constitutive law you are using at each step.

notes.h: Stress, strain and Hooke's law in three dimensions
notes.body:
To analyse any solid we need to describe the internal forces (stress), the deformation (strain) and the link between them (the constitutive law).

Stress at a point
- On a small cube aligned with x, y, z there are three direct stresses (σx, σy, σz) and shear stresses (τxy, τyz, τzx and their partners).
- Moment equilibrium of the cube shows τxy = τyx, τyz = τzy and τzx = τxz, so the stress state has six independent components.
- Sign convention: tensile direct stress is positive.

Strain
- Direct strain: εx = ∂u/∂x, εy = ∂v/∂y, εz = ∂w/∂z, where u, v, w are displacements.
- Engineering shear strain: γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x (the change in a right angle, in radians), and similarly γyz and γzx.

Generalised Hooke's law (linear, isotropic material)
- εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E
- εy = [σy − ν(σz + σx)]/E
- εz = [σz − ν(σx + σy)]/E
- γxy = τxy/G, γyz = τyz/G, γzx = τzx/G
- Only two constants are independent: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]. The bulk modulus is K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)].
- Volumetric strain ≈ εx + εy + εz = (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy + σz)/E.

Worked example (aluminium, E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3) with σx = 100 MPa, σy = 50 MPa, σz = 0:
- εx = (100 − 0.3 × 50)/70 000 = 1.21 × 10⁻³
- εy = (50 − 0.3 × 100)/70 000 = 2.86 × 10⁻⁴
- εz = −0.3 × 150/70 000 = −6.43 × 10⁻⁴ (the plate gets thinner even though σz = 0)
- G = 70/2.6 ≈ 26.9 GPa.

Plane stress and plane strain
- Plane stress (thin plates and skins): σz = τxz = τyz = 0, but εz is not zero.
- Plane strain (long bodies restrained along z): εz = 0, so σz = ν(σx + σy) is not zero.

Principal stresses and Mohr's circle (2D)
- Centre (σx + σy)/2, radius R = √{[(σx − σy)/2]² + τxy²}.
- Principal stresses σ1,2 = centre ± R; maximum in-plane shear = R.
- Principal direction: tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx − σy).
- Example: σx = 80, σy = 20, τxy = 40 MPa gives centre 50, R = 50, so σ1 = 100 MPa, σ2 = 0, and θp ≈ 26.6°.

Exam tips: a common slip is to forget the Poisson terms, giving εz = 0 in plane stress. Always check that your strains satisfy the volumetric-strain identity as a quick arithmetic check.

notes.h: Pin-jointed frameworks and the principle of virtual work
notes.body:
A pin-jointed framework (truss) is an idealisation in which straight members are joined by frictionless pins and loads act only at the joints. Each member then carries only an axial force: tension (positive) or compression.

Statical determinacy
- For a plane framework with m members, r reaction components and j joints: m + r = 2j is necessary for statical determinacy.
- For a space framework: m + r = 3j.
- m + r < 2j means a mechanism; m + r > 2j means the framework is redundant (indeterminate).
- The count is necessary but not sufficient: members must also be arranged so the frame is not a mechanism (check the geometry).

Finding member forces
- Method of joints: equilibrium of each pin (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0). Start at a joint with at most two unknowns.
- Method of sections: cut through no more than three members with unknown forces and take moments about the intersection of two of them to find the third directly.
- Assume all unknown forces are tensile; a negative answer then means compression.

Deflections: the unit load method
The principle of virtual forces (complementary virtual work) says: for a compatible set of real displacements and any set of virtual forces in equilibrium, external virtual work equals internal virtual work. Applying a virtual unit load at the joint and in the direction where we want the displacement δ gives:

1 × δ = Σ (F f L)/(A E)

- F = real force in each member under the actual loads.
- f = force in each member due to the unit load alone.
- L, A, E = member length, area and Young's modulus. FL/AE is the member's real extension.

Worked example
Joint C is supported by a horizontal tie AC (length L) and a strut BC at 45° (length √2 L), both fixed to a wall. A load W hangs from C.
- Equilibrium at C: BC carries W√2 in compression, AC carries W in tension.
- For the vertical deflection of C, the unit load is also vertical, so f = F/W: f_AC = 1, f_BC = −√2.
- δ = [W(1)L + (−W√2)(−√2)(√2 L)]/(AE) = (1 + 2√2)WL/AE ≈ 3.83 WL/AE.
- With W = 10 kN, L = 1 m, A = 100 mm², E = 70 GPa: AE = 7.0 MN, so δ ≈ 3.83 × 10 000 × 1000/7.0 × 10⁶ ≈ 5.47 mm downwards.
- For the horizontal deflection, a horizontal unit load at C gives f_AC = 1 and f_BC = 0, so δh = WL/AE ≈ 1.43 mm.

Why virtual work?
It replaces messy geometry (finding where member ends move to) with a simple sum, and it extends directly to beams (∫Mm dx/EI) and to redundant structures.

Exam tips: tabulate member, L, F, f and FfL for every member; keep signs (tension positive) throughout; a zero-force member under the unit load contributes nothing even if it is heavily loaded.

A redundant framework has more members or supports than equilibrium needs (m + r > 2j in 2D). Equilibrium alone cannot fix the member forces because the load can share itself between alternative paths in different proportions; the stiffer path takes more.

Why build redundant structures?
- Fail-safe design: if one member fails the load can find another path. This is a central idea in aircraft damage tolerance.
- Greater stiffness for the same weight in some layouts.
- The price: forces depend on member stiffnesses, and temperature changes or lack of fit cause stresses even with no external load (self-straining).

The force method (one redundant)
1. Choose one redundant member and imagine it cut (released), leaving a determinate "primary" structure.
2. Find the member forces F₀ in the primary structure under the real loads.
3. Find the member forces f₁ in the primary structure due to a pair of unit tensile forces applied at the cut.
4. Compatibility: the two cut faces must not separate. The relative movement across the cut is Σ F₀ f₁ L/(AE) from the loads plus R Σ f₁² L/(AE) from the redundant force R. Setting the total to zero:
   R = −Σ (F₀ f₁ L/AE) / Σ (f₁² L/AE)
5. Final forces: F = F₀ + R f₁.
Include the redundant member itself in the sums (it has F₀ = 0 and f₁ = 1).

Classic example: three-bar symmetric framework
A vertical bar (length L) and two bars inclined at θ to it meet at a joint carrying a vertical load P; all have the same AE.
- Compatibility: if the joint moves down by δ, the vertical bar extends by δ and each inclined bar by δ cos θ.
- Constitutive: F₁ = AEδ/L; F₂ = AE(δ cos θ)/(L/cos θ) = F₁ cos² θ.
- Equilibrium: F₁ + 2F₂ cos θ = P.
- Result: F₁ = P/(1 + 2cos³θ) and F₂ = P cos²θ/(1 + 2cos³θ).
- For θ = 45°: F₁ ≈ 0.586P, F₂ ≈ 0.293P (check: 0.586 + 2 × 0.293 × 0.707 = 1.000).
Note the vertical bar, being shorter and better aligned, takes the largest share.

Temperature and lack of fit
- A bar fixed between rigid walls and heated by ΔT wants to grow by αΔT L. Fully restrained, it carries σ = −EαΔT. For steel (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K) with ΔT = 50 K, σ = −120 MPa (compressive).
- Lack of fit is treated the same way: the compatibility equation gains a term equal to the initial gap or misfit.

Exam tips: state clearly which member you release and your sign convention for R; always include the redundant member in Σ f₁²L/AE; finish by checking equilibrium at a joint with the final forces.

The engineer's (Euler–Bernoulli) theory of bending gives the direct stress in a beam carrying a bending moment. It underpins almost all beam and wing-spar sizing in Year 1.

Assumptions
- The beam is initially straight, and the material is homogeneous, isotropic and linear elastic.
- Plane cross-sections remain plane and normal to the deformed axis (shear deformation is neglected).
- Deflections are small.
- The section is symmetric about the plane of loading (the unsymmetric case is treated in the final topic of this pack).

Derivation in outline
- Compatibility: if the neutral surface is bent to radius R, a fibre at distance y from it has strain ε = y/R (tension on the convex side).
- Constitutive: σ = Eε = Ey/R.
- Equilibrium (axial): ∫σ dA = 0 means ∫y dA = 0, so the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the section.
- Equilibrium (moment): M = ∫σy dA = (E/R)∫y² dA = EI/R.
- Combining: σ/y = M/I = E/R.

Key result
σ = My/I, with the maximum stress at the extreme fibre: σmax = M/Z where Z = I/y_max is the elastic section modulus.

Second moments of area
- Rectangle b × h about its centroidal axis: I = bh³/12.
- Solid circle of diameter d: I = πd⁴/64.
- Parallel axis theorem: I = I_c + A d², where d is the distance from the part's own centroid to the reference axis.
- Material far from the neutral axis does most of the work, which is why I-beams, spar caps and skin–stringer panels concentrate area at the extremes.

Worked example
A rectangular section 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep carries M = 10 kN m.
- I = 50 × 100³/12 = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
- y_max = 50 mm, so σmax = 10 × 10⁶ × 50/4.17 × 10⁶ = 120 MPa (tension on one face, compression on the other).
- Z = 8.33 × 10⁴ mm³.
If the same rectangle were placed flat (100 wide, 50 deep), I = 100 × 50³/12 = 1.04 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and σmax would double to 240 MPa.

Curvature
1/R = M/EI: EI is the flexural rigidity and controls how much the beam bends. This links directly to the deflection topic.

Exam tips: always locate the centroid before computing I; use consistent units (N and mm give MPa); state which face is in tension. If the section is not symmetric about the loading plane, the simple σ = My/I formula does not apply.

notes.h: Shear force and bending moment diagrams
notes.body:
Before you can find stresses or deflections in a beam you need the internal shear force Q (also written V or S) and bending moment M at every section. These come from equilibrium of a free body cut from the beam.

Sign convention (state yours in the exam)
- A common convention: sagging bending moment is positive (top in compression); shear force is positive when it tends to rotate the cut element clockwise.
- With downward distributed load w per unit length: dQ/dx = −w and dM/dx = Q.

Consequences of the relations
- Where there is no distributed load, Q is constant and M varies linearly.
- Under a uniform load, Q varies linearly and M is a parabola.
- A point load causes a step in Q; a point (couple) moment causes a step in M.
- M has a maximum or minimum where Q = 0 (or where Q changes sign at a point load).
- The change in M between two sections equals the area of the Q diagram between them.

Standard results
- Simply supported, span L, central point load P: reactions P/2, Mmax = PL/4 at mid-span.
- Simply supported, uniform load w: reactions wL/2, Mmax = wL²/8 at mid-span.
- Cantilever, tip load P: Q = P throughout, Mmax = PL (hogging) at the root.
- Cantilever, uniform load w: Mmax = wL²/2 at the root.

Method
1. Find support reactions from equilibrium of the whole beam (ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0).
2. Cut at a general section x in each region between load discontinuities. Write Q(x) and M(x) from the free body to one side.
3. Plot, marking values at supports, load points and turning points.
4. Check: M = 0 at free ends and pin/roller supports (unless a couple acts there).

Worked example
A simply supported beam of span 5 m carries a uniform load of 4 kN/m.
- Reactions: R = wL/2 = 10 kN at each end.
- Q(x) = 10 − 4x kN, zero at x = 2.5 m.
- M(x) = 10x − 2x² kN m; at x = 2.5 m, M = 25 − 12.5 = 12.5 kN m, which equals wL²/8.

Aircraft link
A wing behaves like a cantilever from the fuselage: lift acts upward along the span, while wing weight, fuel and engines act downward and relieve the root bending moment. This "inertia relief" is why fuel is often used from the centre tanks first.

Exam tips: always draw the free-body diagram with reactions shown; label peak values and their positions; use the area-under-Q rule as a check rather than as your only method.

Stiffness requirements often govern aircraft structures, so we need the deflected shape of a beam, not just its stresses.

The governing equation
From M = EI/R and, for small slopes, 1/R ≈ d²v/dx²:
EI d²v/dx² = M(x)
(with v measured upwards and sagging moment positive; some texts measure v downwards and write EI v'' = −M, so state your convention).
- Integrate once for the slope dv/dx, twice for the deflection v.
- Find the constants from the boundary conditions.

Boundary conditions
- Built-in (clamped) end: v = 0 and dv/dx = 0.
- Pinned or roller support: v = 0 (and M = 0).
- Free end: M = 0 and Q = 0 (these are used when integrating from the load, w, rather than from M).

Macaulay's method
When the loading has several discontinuities, write one expression for M(x) using Macaulay brackets ⟨x − a⟩, which equal zero when x < a and (x − a) when x ≥ a. Integrate the brackets as if they were ordinary terms: ∫⟨x − a⟩ⁿ dx = ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1). This gives a single pair of integration constants for the whole beam.

Standard results (magnitudes)
- Cantilever, tip load P: tip deflection PL³/(3EI), tip slope PL²/(2EI).
- Cantilever, uniform load w: tip deflection wL⁴/(8EI).
- Simply supported, central load P: mid-span deflection PL³/(48EI).
- Simply supported, uniform load w: mid-span deflection 5wL⁴/(384EI).

Worked example
An aluminium cantilever (E = 70 GPa) of length 2 m has the 50 × 100 mm rectangular section (I = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴) and carries a 1 kN tip load.
- EI = 70 000 × 4.17 × 10⁶ ≈ 2.92 × 10¹¹ N mm².
- δ = PL³/(3EI) = 1000 × 2000³/(3 × 2.92 × 10¹¹) ≈ 9.1 mm.
Doubling the length multiplies the deflection by 8, because of the L³ term.

Virtual work for beams
The unit load method extends to beams: δ = ∫ M m dx/(EI), where M is the real moment and m the moment due to a unit load at the point and in the direction of δ. For the cantilever above, M = −Px and m = −x (x from the tip), so δ = ∫₀ᴸ Px² dx/EI = PL³/(3EI), matching the standard result.

Superposition
For linear elastic beams, deflections due to separate loads can be added. This is the quickest route in many exam questions and is the basis of the method for indeterminate beams.

Exam tips: check units (N, mm, MPa give mm); sanity-check the sign of your deflection; quote standard results only when the question allows, otherwise derive them by integration.

A beam is statically indeterminate when it has more support reactions than the equilibrium equations can find (three for a plane beam: ΣFx, ΣFy, ΣM; usually two once axial loads are absent). Examples: the propped cantilever (one redundant) and the built-in (fixed–fixed) beam (two redundants for transverse loading).

Approach 1: superposition (force method)
1. Remove enough supports to leave a determinate "released" beam.
2. Compute the deflection (or slope) at each removed support due to the applied loads.
3. Compute the deflection due to the unknown redundant reaction acting alone.
4. Compatibility: the total deflection (or slope) at the real support must be zero. Solve for the redundant.

Example: propped cantilever with uniform load w
- Remove the prop. The cantilever tip deflects down by wL⁴/(8EI).
- The prop force R pushes the tip up by RL³/(3EI).
- Compatibility: RL³/(3EI) = wL⁴/(8EI), so R = 3wL/8.
- Root reaction = 5wL/8; root moment = wL²/8 (hogging).
- Maximum sagging moment = 9wL²/128 at 3L/8 from the prop.

Approach 2: integration with extra boundary conditions
Write M(x) including the unknown reaction, integrate EI v'' = M twice, and use all the boundary conditions. A propped cantilever gives three conditions (v = 0 and v' = 0 at the root, v = 0 at the prop) for two integration constants and one unknown reaction.

Approach 3: virtual work
Release the redundant, then R = −∫M₀ m dx/∫m² dx, where M₀ is the moment in the released beam and m the moment from a unit redundant. This is the same structure as the redundant-framework formula.

Standard results worth knowing
- Built-in beam, uniform load w: end moments wL²/12 (hogging), mid-span moment wL²/24 (sagging), mid-span deflection wL⁴/(384EI), five times smaller than for simple supports.
- Built-in beam, central point load P: end moments PL/8, mid-span moment PL/8, deflection PL³/(192EI).
- Propped cantilever, central point load P: prop reaction 5P/16, root moment 3PL/16.

Why it matters
Indeterminate beams are stiffer and have lower peak moments than determinate ones, but they are sensitive to support settlement and temperature changes, and their internal forces depend on the relative stiffness (EI) of the parts.

Exam tips: state the compatibility condition in words before writing it as an equation; check your answer with overall equilibrium (the reactions must sum to the total load); sketch the bending moment diagram showing both hogging and sagging regions and the point of contraflexure.

Shafts transmitting power (engine and propeller shafts, helicopter rotor drives, control rods) carry torque. Circular sections are the simplest case because cross-sections stay plane and simply rotate.

Assumptions
- Straight shaft of uniform circular (solid or hollow) section, linear elastic, homogeneous material.
- Plane cross-sections remain plane and radii remain straight: each section rotates as a rigid disc.
- Small twist angles.

Derivation in outline
- Compatibility: a line on the surface of length L twists so that a section rotates by θ relative to the other end. The shear strain at radius r is γ = rθ/L.
- Constitutive: τ = Gγ = Grθ/L, so shear stress grows linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the outer surface.
- Equilibrium: T = ∫τ r dA = (Gθ/L)∫r² dA = GJθ/L, where J = ∫r² dA is the polar second moment of area.

The torsion formula
T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L
- Solid shaft of diameter d: J = πd⁴/32.
- Hollow shaft, outer D and inner d: J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.
- GJ is the torsional rigidity; θ = TL/(GJ).

Worked example
A solid shaft of diameter 50 mm carries a torque of 2 kN m. Take G = 27 GPa (an aluminium alloy) and length 1 m.
- J = π × 50⁴/32 ≈ 6.14 × 10⁵ mm⁴.
- τmax = Tr/J = 2 × 10⁶ × 25/6.14 × 10⁵ ≈ 81.5 MPa.
- θ = TL/(GJ) = 2 × 10⁶ × 1000/(27 000 × 6.14 × 10⁵) ≈ 0.121 rad ≈ 6.9°.

Hollow shafts are efficient
Material near the centre carries little stress. A tube with D = 50 mm and d = 40 mm uses only 36% of the material of the solid 50 mm shaft but keeps about 59% of its J. Under the same 2 kN m torque its peak stress rises to about 138 MPa, still often acceptable, for a large weight saving.

Power transmission
P = Tω, with ω in rad/s. For example, 2 kN m at 3000 rpm (ω = 314 rad/s) transmits about 628 kW.

Shafts in series and parallel
- In series (different sections end to end), the torque is the same in each part and the twists add.
- In parallel (e.g. a shaft built in at both ends with a torque applied part-way along), the twists are equal and the torques share in proportion to GJ/L: a statically indeterminate problem solved exactly like the axially loaded bar.

Non-circular sections
For non-circular sections plane sections warp and T/J = τ/r no longer applies. Thin-walled closed tubes are usually treated with shear flow (the Bredt–Batho formula) in a later structures course.

Exam tips: keep units consistent (N mm and mm give MPa); use the outer radius for the peak stress; convert rpm to rad/s (× 2π/60) for power questions.

Many aircraft sections (Z-section stringers, angle sections, wing boxes with unequal flanges) are not symmetric about the plane of loading. For these, σ = My/I gives wrong answers: a moment about one axis also bends the beam about the other.

Section properties
- Ixx = ∫y² dA, Iyy = ∫x² dA and the product second moment Ixy = ∫xy dA, all about axes through the centroid.
- Ixy = 0 if either axis is an axis of symmetry. For a Z or angle section Ixy ≠ 0.
- Thin-walled approximation: treat the wall as a line of thickness t and neglect terms in t³ (e.g. a horizontal flange's own Ixx about its centreline, bt³/12).
- Parallel axis theorem for the product: Ixy = Ixy,c + A x̄ ȳ for each part.

Direct stress under unsymmetric bending
With Mx and My about centroidal axes (sign convention: positive Mx causes tension where y is positive, positive My causes tension where x is positive):
σ = [(My Ixx − Mx Ixy) x + (Mx Iyy − My Ixy) y]/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²)
For Mx only (My = 0):
σ = Mx (Iyy y − Ixy x)/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²)
This reduces to σ = Mx y/Ixx when Ixy = 0.

Neutral axis
Set σ = 0. For Mx only: y = (Ixy/Iyy) x, a line through the centroid inclined at tan⁻¹(Ixy/Iyy) to the x axis. The neutral axis is not perpendicular to the plane of the applied moment, and the beam deflects partly sideways.

Worked example: Z-section
Web 100 mm deep, flanges 50 mm wide (top flange to the right, bottom flange to the left), uniform thickness 2 mm. The centroid is at the middle of the web.
- Ixx ≈ 2 × 100³/12 + 2 × (50 × 2) × 50² = 1.67 × 10⁵ + 5.00 × 10⁵ = 6.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴.
- Iyy ≈ 2 × [2 × 50³/12 + (50 × 2) × 25²] = 1.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴.
- Ixy ≈ (100 × 25 × 50) + (100 × (−25) × (−50)) = 2.50 × 10⁵ mm⁴.
- Ixx Iyy − Ixy² ≈ 4.86 × 10¹⁰ mm⁸.
For Mx = 1 kN m:
- At the web–top flange corner (0, 50): σ = +171 MPa.
- At the top flange tip (50, 50): σ = −86 MPa: compression, even though it is in the "tension" half of the section.
- The naive answer Mx y/Ixx = 75 MPa is badly wrong.
- Neutral axis: slope Ixy/Iyy = 1.5, i.e. about 56° to the x axis.

Shear flow and shear centre (introduction)
In thin walls the shear stress from a shear force is described by the shear flow q = τt (force per unit length of wall), which is found by integrating along the wall from a free edge. The resultant of the shear flows passes through the shear centre; a load applied elsewhere also twists the section. For channel and angle sections the shear centre does not coincide with the centroid (for an angle it is at the corner where the legs meet), which is why stringer and spar design must account for twist. A Z-section with equal flanges is point-symmetric, so its shear centre is at the centroid.

Exam tips: compute the centroid first, tabulate A, x̄, ȳ for each wall element, keep track of the sign of Ixy, and check your stress formula by setting Ixy = 0.

cards.b: The maximum load expected in service. The structure must carry it without detrimental permanent deformation.
Limit load multiplied by the factor of safety (1.5 for civil transport aircraft under CS-25/FAR 25). The structure must carry it without failure.
Equilibrium (forces and moments balance), compatibility (deformations fit together and match supports) and the constitutive law (stress–strain relation, e.g. σ = Eε).
One whose internal forces and reactions can all be found from equilibrium alone, without considering deformation.
Young's modulus divided by density, E/ρ. Used to compare materials for weight-critical stiffness design; aluminium, steel and titanium are all about 25 MJ/kg.

cards.f: Why stiffness matters as well as strength in aircraft
cards.b: Excessive deflection changes aerodynamic shape and can cause aeroelastic problems such as flutter, divergence or loss of control effectiveness, even when stresses are safe.

cards.f: Number of independent stress components at a point
cards.b: Six: three direct stresses and three shear stresses, because moment equilibrium of an element gives τxy = τyx, τyz = τzy and τzx = τxz.
εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E for a linear elastic isotropic material.

cards.f: Relation between E, G and ν
cards.b: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]. For aluminium (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3) G ≈ 26.9 GPa.
γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x: the reduction in the right angle between lines originally along x and y, in radians.
Plane stress: σz = 0 but εz ≠ 0 (thin plates). Plane strain: εz = 0 but σz = ν(σx + σy) ≠ 0 (long restrained bodies).
R = √{[(σx − σy)/2]² + τxy²}; principal stresses are (σx + σy)/2 ± R and the maximum in-plane shear stress is R.
K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)]; relates mean stress to volumetric strain. As ν → 0.5 the material becomes incompressible.
Frictionless pin joints, straight members, loads applied only at joints, so every member carries only axial force (tension or compression).

cards.f: Determinacy condition for a plane truss
cards.b: m + r = 2j (members + reactions = 2 × joints). Necessary but not sufficient: the geometry must also not form a mechanism.

cards.f: Determinacy condition for a space truss
cards.b: m + r = 3j, since each joint gives three equilibrium equations.

cards.f: Unit load method for truss deflection
cards.b: δ = Σ F f L/(AE): F is the real member force, f the member force from a unit load applied where (and in the direction) δ is wanted.
Cut the truss through at most three unknown members and use equilibrium of one part; take moments about the intersection of two unknown members to find the third directly.
For real compatible displacements and any virtual force system in equilibrium, external virtual work = internal virtual work. Basis of the unit load method.
A member that can be removed without the framework becoming a mechanism; its force cannot be found from equilibrium alone.
R = −Σ(F₀ f₁ L/AE)/Σ(f₁² L/AE), with the redundant member included in both sums; final forces F = F₀ + R f₁.
Stresses in a redundant structure caused by temperature change or lack of fit, with no external load. Impossible in a determinate structure.
σ = −EαΔT (compressive). Steel, ΔT = 50 K: about −120 MPa.

cards.f: Three-bar framework, equal AE, outer bars at θ
cards.b: Central bar F₁ = P/(1 + 2cos³θ); outer bars F₂ = P cos²θ/(1 + 2cos³θ). At 45°: 0.586P and 0.293P.
Providing alternative load paths (redundancy) so that if one member or element fails the structure can still carry the required load until the damage is found.
σ = My/I, with y measured from the neutral axis; σmax = M/Z, where Z = I/y_max.

cards.f: Where the neutral axis lies (pure bending, elastic)
cards.b: Through the centroid of the cross-section, because axial equilibrium requires ∫y dA = 0.

cards.f: Second moment of area of a rectangle
cards.b: I = bh³/12 about the centroidal axis parallel to b (h is the depth in the plane of bending).
I = I_c + A d²: second moment about any axis = value about the parallel centroidal axis + area × (distance between axes)².

cards.f: Key assumption of engineer's bending theory
cards.b: Plane sections remain plane and normal to the neutral axis; strain varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis (ε = y/R).
M = EI/R, i.e. curvature 1/R = M/(EI). EI is the flexural rigidity.

cards.f: Relation between load, shear and moment
cards.b: dQ/dx = −w and dM/dx = Q (with downward load w and sagging moment positive). So M is extreme where Q = 0.

cards.f: Max moment: simply supported beam, uniform load w
cards.b: wL²/8 at mid-span; reactions wL/2.

cards.f: Max moment: simply supported beam, central point load P
cards.b: PL/4 at mid-span; reactions P/2.

cards.f: Max moment: cantilever with tip load P
cards.b: PL (hogging) at the built-in root; shear force P constant along the beam.

cards.f: Effect of a point load on the diagrams
cards.b: A step change in the shear force diagram (equal to the load) and a kink (change of slope) in the bending moment diagram.
The change in bending moment between two sections equals the area under the shear force diagram between them.
Downward wing weight, fuel and engine loads oppose lift and reduce the root shear force and bending moment.
EI d²v/dx² = M(x) for small slopes (v upwards, sagging M positive). Integrate twice and apply boundary conditions.

cards.f: Boundary conditions at a built-in end
cards.b: Deflection v = 0 and slope dv/dx = 0.

cards.f: Cantilever tip deflection under a tip load
cards.b: δ = PL³/(3EI); tip slope PL²/(2EI).

cards.f: Simply supported beam, uniform load: centre deflection
cards.b: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI).

cards.f: Simply supported beam, central point load: centre deflection
cards.b: δ = PL³/(48EI).
Zero for x < a and (x − a) for x ≥ a; lets one moment expression cover a beam with several load discontinuities and be integrated term by term.
δ = ∫ M m dx/(EI): M from real loads, m from a unit load applied at the point and in the direction of the required deflection.

cards.f: Propped cantilever with uniform load: prop reaction
cards.b: R = 3wL/8 (from wL⁴/8EI = RL³/3EI). Root reaction 5wL/8, root moment wL²/8.

cards.f: Built-in beam, uniform load: end and mid-span moments
cards.b: End moments wL²/12 (hogging); mid-span moment wL²/24 (sagging).

cards.f: Built-in beam, uniform load: mid-span deflection
cards.b: wL⁴/(384EI), one fifth of the simply supported value 5wL⁴/(384EI).
A point where the bending moment changes sign (passes through zero), so the curvature of the beam reverses.

cards.f: Superposition method for an indeterminate beam
cards.b: Remove redundant supports, find the deflection there from the loads, add the deflection from the unknown reaction, and set the total equal to the real support condition (usually zero).

cards.f: Propped cantilever with central point load: prop reaction
cards.b: 5P/16; root moment 3PL/16.
T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L for a circular shaft: shear stress varies linearly with radius and twist θ = TL/(GJ).

cards.f: Polar second moment of area, solid circle
cards.b: J = πd⁴/32. For a hollow circle J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.
GJ: torque per unit twist per unit length. Twist angle θ = TL/(GJ).
P = Tω, with ω in rad/s (rpm × 2π/60).
Material near the axis carries little shear stress, so removing it saves much weight but only a little torsional stiffness and strength.
Same torque in each part; total twist = sum of TL/(GJ) for each part.

cards.f: Why T/J = τ/r fails for non-circular sections
cards.b: Non-circular sections warp out of plane under torque, so the 'plane sections remain plane' assumption is invalid.
Ixy = ∫xy dA about centroidal axes. Zero if either axis is an axis of symmetry; non-zero for Z and angle sections.

cards.f: Direct stress for Mx only, unsymmetric section
cards.b: σ = Mx(Iyy y − Ixy x)/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²), with Mx positive causing tension at positive y.

cards.f: Neutral axis for Mx only, unsymmetric section
cards.b: y = (Ixy/Iyy)x: inclined to the x axis, so it is not perpendicular to the plane of the moment.
Represent walls by their mid-line with thickness t and neglect terms in t² and t³ compared with terms in t.
q = τt: shear force per unit length along a thin wall. Found by integrating from a free edge where q = 0.
The point through which a shear load must act to produce bending without twisting. For channel and angle sections it is not at the centroid; for an equal-flange Z it is (point symmetry).

questions.q: A transport aircraft's limit load case gives a wing root bending moment of 4.0 MN m. Using the standard civil factor of safety, what bending moment must the wing carry without failure?
questions.why: Ultimate load is limit load × 1.5, so 4.0 × 1.5 = 6.0 MN m. 4.0 MN m is the limit load itself, which the wing must carry without permanent deformation, not the failure requirement. 2.7 MN m comes from dividing by 1.5 instead of multiplying. 8.0 MN m uses a factor of 2, which is not the standard civil aircraft factor.

questions.q: Using E ≈ 70 GPa and ρ ≈ 2700 kg/m³ for aluminium and E ≈ 200 GPa and ρ ≈ 7850 kg/m³ for steel, which statement about specific stiffness is correct?
options: They are almost the same, about 25–26 MJ/kg
Steel is nearly three times stiffer per unit mass
Aluminium is nearly three times stiffer per unit mass
Steel is about 2.9 times stiffer, so it is always lighter for a stiffness-limited part
questions.why: E/ρ is 70×10⁹/2700 ≈ 25.9 MJ/kg for aluminium and 200×10⁹/7850 ≈ 25.5 MJ/kg for steel, so they are nearly equal. 'Steel nearly three times stiffer per unit mass' compares E alone (200/70 ≈ 2.9) and forgets to divide by density. 'Aluminium nearly three times stiffer' wrongly compares density ratios (7850/2700 ≈ 2.9) as if they were stiffness. The statement that steel is always lighter for a stiffness-limited part repeats the E-only error and draws a false design conclusion from it.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a statically determinate and a statically indeterminate structure, and state what extra information is needed to analyse the second type.
markScheme: Determinate: reactions and internal forces found from equilibrium alone
Indeterminate: more unknowns than independent equilibrium equations (redundants)
Needs compatibility conditions (deformations must fit together / match supports)
Needs a constitutive law (e.g. σ = Eε, member stiffness AE/L) to link forces to deformations
questions.modelAnswer: A statically determinate structure has exactly as many unknown reactions and internal forces as there are independent equilibrium equations, so equilibrium alone gives every force. A statically indeterminate structure has more unknowns than equations; the extra unknowns are called redundants. To find them we add compatibility conditions, which say how the deformations of members must fit together or match the supports, and a constitutive law (for elastic members σ = Eε, so a bar's extension is FL/AE) to turn those deformation conditions into equations in the forces.

questions.q: A thin aluminium plate (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3) carries σx = 100 MPa and σy = 50 MPa with no other stresses. What is the through-thickness strain εz?
questions.why: εz = −ν(σx + σy)/E = −0.3 × 150/70 000 = −6.43 × 10⁻⁴. Zero is wrong because plane stress sets σz to zero, not εz. −2.14 × 10⁻⁴ uses only σy in the Poisson term (−0.3 × 50/70 000) and ignores the contribution of σx. +8.57 × 10⁻⁴ is the volumetric strain (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy)/E, which is a different quantity.

questions.q: A 2D stress state has σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 40 MPa. What is the major principal stress?
questions.why: Centre = (80 + 20)/2 = 50 MPa; radius = √(30² + 40²) = 50 MPa, so σ1 = 50 + 50 = 100 MPa. 80 MPa is just σx, which ignores the shear stress (it would be a principal stress only if τxy were zero). 122 MPa uses the full difference σx − σy = 60 MPa instead of half of it in the radius, giving R = √(60² + 40²) ≈ 72 MPa. 50 MPa is the centre of Mohr's circle (the mean in-plane stress), which also happens to equal the maximum shear stress here, but it is not the major principal stress.

questions.q: Starting from the generalised Hooke's law, show that the volumetric strain of a linear elastic isotropic material under stresses σx, σy, σz is (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy + σz)/E, and explain what happens as ν approaches 0.5.
markScheme: Writes the three direct-strain equations correctly
Adds them: the σ terms collect to (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy + σz)/E
States that volumetric strain ≈ εx + εy + εz for small strains
As ν → 0.5 the factor (1 − 2ν) → 0, so volume change → 0
Interprets this as incompressible behaviour (e.g. rubber); K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)] → ∞
questions.modelAnswer: For small strains the change in volume per unit volume is εx + εy + εz. Using Hooke's law, εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E, εy = [σy − ν(σz + σx)]/E and εz = [σz − ν(σx + σy)]/E. Adding, each stress appears once with coefficient 1 and twice with coefficient −ν, so the sum is (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy + σz)/E. As ν tends to 0.5 the factor (1 − 2ν) tends to zero, so the material changes shape but not volume: it is incompressible, and its bulk modulus K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)] tends to infinity. Rubber-like materials behave close to this.

questions.q: A plane truss has 10 members and 6 joints and is supported by a pin (2 reactions) and a roller (1 reaction). Assuming the members are arranged so that it is not a mechanism, how should it be classified?
options: Statically indeterminate to the second degree
Statically indeterminate to the first degree
questions.why: m + r = 10 + 3 = 13 while 2j = 12, so there is one more unknown than there are equilibrium equations: indeterminate to the first degree. 'Statically determinate' comes from counting the pin as only one reaction (10 + 2 = 12). 'A mechanism' comes from using the space-frame rule 3j = 18, which is for 3D trusses. 'Second degree' comes from counting the roller as two reactions (10 + 4 − 12 = 2); a roller only provides one.

questions.q: Joint C is held by a horizontal tie (length 1 m) and a 45° strut (length √2 m), with W = 10 kN hanging from C. Both members have A = 100 mm² and E = 70 GPa. What is the vertical deflection of C?
questions.why: Tie force +W, strut force −W√2; unit-load forces +1 and −√2. δ = (1 + 2√2)WL/AE = 3.83 × 10 000 × 1000/(7 × 10⁶) ≈ 5.47 mm. 1.43 mm is the tie term alone, which is in fact the horizontal deflection of C. 4.04 mm is the strut term alone (2√2 WL/AE), forgetting the tie's contribution. 4.29 mm uses length L for the strut instead of √2 L, giving (1 + 2)WL/AE.

questions.q: State the principle on which the unit load method rests and derive the expression δ = Σ F f L/(AE) for the deflection of a joint of a pin-jointed framework.
markScheme: States the principle of virtual forces (complementary virtual work): virtual external work = virtual internal work for real compatible displacements
Applies a virtual unit load at the joint in the direction of δ; external virtual work = 1 × δ
Virtual member forces f are in equilibrium with the unit load
Real member extension e = FL/(AE); internal virtual work = Σ f e
Equates to give δ = Σ F f L/(AE)
questions.modelAnswer: The principle of virtual forces states that if a structure undergoes a real, compatible set of displacements, then for any set of virtual forces in equilibrium the work done by the external virtual forces through the real displacements equals the work done by the internal virtual forces through the real deformations. Apply a virtual unit load at the joint, in the direction of the displacement δ we want. Its external virtual work is 1 × δ. The member forces it produces, f, are found by ordinary equilibrium. Each member's real extension is e = FL/(AE), where F is the real force from the actual loads. The internal virtual work is Σ f e. Equating, 1 × δ = Σ F f L/(AE).

questions.q: In a symmetric three-bar framework (equal AE) the outer bars are at 45° to the central vertical bar and a vertical load P acts at the common joint. What force does the central bar carry?
questions.why: F₁ = P/(1 + 2cos³45°) = P/1.707 = 0.586P. 0.333P assumes the three bars share the load equally, ignoring their inclination and different lengths. 0.414P uses cos θ instead of cos³θ in the denominator (P/2.414), which forgets that the outer bars are longer and only partly aligned with the load. 0.293P is the force in each outer bar, not the central one.

questions.q: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per K) is fixed between two rigid walls and heated by 50 K. What stress develops?
options: 0, because there is no external load
questions.why: The bar wants to extend by αΔT L but the walls prevent it, so σ = −EαΔT = −200 000 MPa × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = −120 MPa, compressive. 'Tensile' gets the sign wrong: the walls push the bar back. Zero would only hold if one end were free; the restraint makes the bar redundant, so self-straining occurs. 0.12 MPa comes from taking E as 200 MPa instead of 200 GPa (a factor of 1000 unit slip).

questions.q: A bar of length L and axial stiffness AE is built in at both ends. An axial load P is applied at a point a distance a from the left end (b = L − a from the right end). Find the reactions at each end.
markScheme: Equilibrium: R_A + R_B = P (one equation, two unknowns)
Left segment in tension carries R_A, right segment in compression carries R_B (or equivalent sign convention)
Compatibility: extension of left part = shortening of right part (total length unchanged)
R_A a/(AE) = R_B b/(AE)
R_A = Pb/L and R_B = Pa/L
Comment: stiffer (shorter) segment takes more load
questions.modelAnswer: Let the load act towards the right end. Equilibrium gives R_A + R_B = P, one equation for two unknowns, so the bar is indeterminate to the first degree. The left segment (length a) carries tension R_A and extends by R_A a/AE; the right segment (length b) carries compression R_B and shortens by R_B b/AE. Because the ends are fixed, the total length cannot change, so these must be equal: R_A a = R_B b. Solving with equilibrium, R_A = Pb/L and R_B = Pa/L. The shorter segment is stiffer, so it carries the larger share of the load.

questions.q: A rectangular beam 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep carries a bending moment of 10 kN m about its horizontal centroidal axis. What is the maximum bending stress?
questions.why: I = 50 × 100³/12 = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and σ = My/I = 10⁷ × 50/4.17 × 10⁶ = 120 MPa. 240 MPa is what you get if the rectangle is bent about its weaker axis (b and h swapped). 60 MPa uses y = 25 mm, a quarter of the depth, instead of the extreme fibre at half the depth. 12 MPa comes from taking M as 10⁶ N mm instead of 10⁷ N mm (1 kN m instead of 10 kN m).

questions.q: Two 100 mm × 10 mm flanges are joined by a thin web so that the flange centroids are 200 mm apart. Ignoring the web and the flanges' own second moments, what is I about the centroidal axis?
questions.why: Each flange has A = 1000 mm² at d = 100 mm from the centroid, so I ≈ 2 × 1000 × 100² = 2.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴. 8.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴ uses the full 200 mm spacing as d for both flanges instead of the 100 mm distance to the centroid. 1.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴ counts only one flange. 1.7 × 10⁴ mm⁴ is just the flanges' own bh³/12 terms (2 × 100 × 10³/12), forgetting the parallel axis term A d², which is the dominant part.

questions.q: Derive the bending stress formula σ = My/I from the assumptions of the engineer's theory of bending, showing why the neutral axis passes through the centroid.
markScheme: Plane sections remain plane: ε = y/R (compatibility)
Linear elastic: σ = Ey/R (constitutive)
Axial force zero: ∫σ dA = (E/R)∫y dA = 0 so neutral axis through centroid
Moment: M = ∫σy dA = (E/R)∫y² dA = EI/R
Combine to σ/y = M/I = E/R
questions.modelAnswer: If plane sections remain plane, a beam bent to radius R about its neutral surface has strain ε = y/R in a fibre a distance y from that surface. For a linear elastic material σ = Eε = Ey/R. In pure bending there is no net axial force, so ∫σ dA = (E/R)∫y dA = 0, which means the first moment of area about the neutral axis is zero: the neutral axis passes through the centroid. The internal stresses must also balance the applied moment: M = ∫σ y dA = (E/R)∫y² dA = EI/R. Combining the two expressions gives σ/y = M/I = E/R, so σ = My/I.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 5 m carries a uniform load of 4 kN/m along its whole length. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.why: Mmax = wL²/8 = 4 × 25/8 = 12.5 kN m at mid-span. 25 kN m is wL²/4, which treats the whole load as a central point load (PL/4 with P = wL = 20 kN). 50 kN m is wL²/2, the root moment of a cantilever of the same length. 10 kN m is the support reaction wL/2 (a force in kN), not a moment.

questions.q: Along a length of beam with no distributed load and no point loads, which statement is correct?
options: The shear force is constant and the bending moment varies linearly
The shear force is zero and the bending moment is constant
The shear force varies linearly and the bending moment is parabolic
Both the shear force and the bending moment are constant
questions.why: With w = 0, dQ/dx = 0 so Q is constant, and dM/dx = Q so M is linear in x. 'Shear zero and moment constant' is only the special case of pure bending (Q = 0), not the general result. 'Shear linear and moment parabolic' describes a region with uniform distributed load. 'Both constant' would require Q = 0 for M to be constant, so it is not true in general.

questions.q: A cantilever of length 3 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 2 kN/m over its full length and a point load of 5 kN at the free end. Find the shear force and bending moment at the root and sketch the shape of both diagrams.
markScheme: Root shear = 5 + 2 × 3 = 11 kN
Root moment = 5 × 3 + 2 × 3²/2 = 15 + 9 = 24 kN m (hogging)
Shear varies linearly from 5 kN at the tip to 11 kN at the root
Moment is zero at the tip and varies parabolically to 24 kN m at the root
Correct sign/sense stated
questions.modelAnswer: Measure x from the free end. At a section x the free body to the tip carries the 5 kN point load and 2x kN of distributed load, so Q(x) = 5 + 2x kN, rising linearly from 5 kN at the tip to 11 kN at the root. The moment is M(x) = −(5x + x²) kN m (hogging), zero at the tip and reaching −(15 + 9) = −24 kN m at the root. The shear diagram is a straight line; the moment diagram is a parabola whose slope at the tip equals the 5 kN tip shear and which gets steeper towards the root.

questions.q: An aluminium cantilever (E = 70 GPa, I = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴) is 2 m long and carries a 1 kN load at its tip. What is the tip deflection?
questions.why: δ = PL³/(3EI) = 1000 × 2000³/(3 × 70 000 × 4.17 × 10⁶) ≈ 9.1 mm. 27.4 mm omits the factor of 3 (PL³/EI). 0.57 mm uses the simply supported central-load formula PL³/(48EI), which does not apply to a cantilever. 13.7 mm uses PL³/(2EI), mixing up the deflection with the form of the tip-slope formula PL²/(2EI).

questions.q: If the length of a cantilever carrying a uniformly distributed load w (per unit length) is doubled, with w unchanged, by what factor does the tip deflection increase?
questions.why: δ = wL⁴/(8EI), so doubling L multiplies δ by 2⁴ = 16. A factor of 8 is the result for a fixed tip point load (PL³/3EI), where the total load does not grow with length. A factor of 4 would follow if deflection scaled with L², as the root bending moment wL²/2 does. A factor of 2 assumes deflection is simply proportional to length.

questions.q: By integrating the beam equation, derive the mid-span deflection of a simply supported beam of span L carrying a uniformly distributed load w.
markScheme: M(x) = wLx/2 − wx²/2
EI v' = wLx²/4 − wx³/6 + C₁
EI v = wLx³/12 − wx⁴/24 + C₁x + C₂
v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0; v(L) = 0 (or symmetry v'(L/2) = 0) gives C₁ = −wL³/24
At x = L/2: EI v = −5wL⁴/384, so δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) downwards
questions.modelAnswer: Taking x from the left support, the reactions are wL/2, so M(x) = wLx/2 − wx²/2 (sagging positive). Then EI v'' = M. Integrating: EI v' = wLx²/4 − wx³/6 + C₁ and EI v = wLx³/12 − wx⁴/24 + C₁x + C₂. v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0. By symmetry v'(L/2) = 0: wL³/16 − wL³/48 + C₁ = 0, so C₁ = −wL³/24. At mid-span, EI v = wL⁴/96 − wL⁴/384 − wL⁴/48 = (4 − 1 − 8)wL⁴/384 = −5wL⁴/384. So the mid-span deflection is 5wL⁴/(384EI) downwards.

questions.q: A propped cantilever of span 4 m carries a uniform load of 6 kN/m. What is the reaction at the prop?
questions.why: Compatibility RL³/3EI = wL⁴/8EI gives R = 3wL/8 = 3 × 6 × 4/8 = 9 kN. 12 kN is wL/2, the simply supported reaction, which ignores the extra stiffness of the built-in end. 15 kN is 5wL/8, the reaction at the built-in end, not the prop. 24 kN is the total load wL, which the prop would carry only if the root took nothing.

questions.q: For the same propped cantilever (span 4 m, 6 kN/m), what is the magnitude of the bending moment at the built-in end?
questions.why: Root moment = R × L − wL²/2 = 9 × 4 − 48 = −12 kN m, magnitude wL²/8 = 12 kN m (hogging). 6.75 kN m is the maximum sagging moment, 9wL²/128, which occurs 1.5 m from the prop. 8 kN m is wL²/12, the end moment of a beam built in at both ends. 48 kN m is wL²/2, the root moment of a plain cantilever with no prop.

questions.q: Use superposition to show that the end moments of a beam built in at both ends and carrying a uniform load w are wL²/12.
markScheme: Release end rotations: treat as simply supported beam plus equal end moments M₀ (by symmetry)
End slope of SS beam under UDL: wL³/(24EI)
End slope due to equal end moments M₀ at both ends: M₀L/(2EI)
Compatibility: slopes cancel, so wL³/24 = M₀L/2
M₀ = wL²/12 (hogging)
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the fixed ends by pins and apply unknown end moments M₀, equal at both ends by symmetry. The simply supported beam under w rotates at each end by wL³/(24EI). Equal and opposite end moments M₀ applied at both ends of a simply supported beam produce a constant moment M₀ along it, and each end rotates by M₀L/(2EI) in the opposite sense. The real ends cannot rotate, so wL³/(24EI) = M₀L/(2EI), giving M₀ = wL²/12. These are hogging moments, and the mid-span moment is wL²/8 − wL²/12 = wL²/24 sagging.

questions.q: A solid circular shaft of diameter 50 mm carries a torque of 2 kN m. What is the maximum shear stress?
questions.why: J = π × 50⁴/32 = 6.14 × 10⁵ mm⁴; τ = Tr/J = 2 × 10⁶ × 25/(6.14 × 10⁵) ≈ 81.5 MPa. 163 MPa arises either from using the diameter instead of the radius, or from using the bending second moment I = πd⁴/64 instead of J; both double the answer. 8.15 MPa takes T as 2 × 10⁵ N mm, dropping a factor of 10 when converting kN m to N mm. 0.0815 MPa takes T as 2000 N mm, converting only the kilo prefix and forgetting that 1 m = 1000 mm.

questions.q: A shaft transmits a torque of 2 kN m at 3000 rpm. What power does it transmit?
questions.why: ω = 3000 × 2π/60 = 314 rad/s, so P = Tω = 2000 × 314 ≈ 628 kW. 6.0 MW multiplies the torque by the speed in rpm (2000 × 3000), skipping the conversion to rad/s. 100 kW multiplies by revolutions per second (2000 × 50) and forgets the factor 2π. 37.7 MW multiplies 3000 by 2π but forgets to divide by 60, treating revolutions per minute as revolutions per second.

questions.q: Compare a solid shaft of diameter 50 mm with a hollow shaft of outer diameter 50 mm and inner diameter 40 mm, both carrying 2 kN m. Find the peak shear stress in each and comment on the mass and stiffness.
markScheme: Solid: J = 6.14 × 10⁵ mm⁴, τ ≈ 81.5 MPa
Hollow: J = π(50⁴ − 40⁴)/32 ≈ 3.62 × 10⁵ mm⁴, τ ≈ 138 MPa
Mass ratio hollow/solid = (50² − 40²)/50² = 0.36
Stiffness (GJ) ratio ≈ 0.59
Comment: large weight saving for a modest loss of stiffness; check stress against allowable and buckling of thin tubes
questions.modelAnswer: For the solid shaft J = π × 50⁴/32 = 6.14 × 10⁵ mm⁴ and τmax = 2 × 10⁶ × 25/6.14 × 10⁵ ≈ 81.5 MPa. For the tube J = π(50⁴ − 40⁴)/32 ≈ 3.62 × 10⁵ mm⁴, so τmax = 2 × 10⁶ × 25/3.62 × 10⁵ ≈ 138 MPa. The tube's mass is proportional to its area, (50² − 40²)/50² = 0.36 of the solid shaft, while its torsional stiffness GJ is 0.59 of the solid value. So removing the lightly stressed core saves 64% of the mass for a 41% loss in stiffness and a 69% rise in peak stress; the tube is far more efficient per kilogram, provided the higher stress is acceptable and the wall is not so thin that it buckles.

questions.q: A thin Z-section has Ixx = 6.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴, Iyy = 1.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴ and Ixy = 2.50 × 10⁵ mm⁴ about centroidal axes. It carries Mx = 1 kN m only. What is the direct stress at the point (x, y) = (0, 50 mm)?
questions.why: σ = Mx(Iyy y − Ixy x)/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²) = 10⁶ × (1.67 × 10⁵ × 50)/(4.86 × 10¹⁰) ≈ +171 MPa. +75 MPa is Mx y/Ixx, the symmetric-section formula that ignores Ixy. −86 MPa is the stress at the flange tip (50, 50), not at (0, 50). +300 MPa is Mx y/Iyy, which uses the wrong second moment.

questions.q: For the same Z-section under Mx only, what is the angle between the neutral axis and the x axis?
questions.why: Setting σ = 0 gives y = (Ixy/Iyy)x with Ixy/Iyy = 2.50/1.67 = 1.5, so the angle is tan⁻¹1.5 ≈ 56°. 0° assumes the neutral axis lies along the x axis, which is only true when Ixy = 0. About 21° uses Ixy/Ixx = 0.375 (tan⁻¹0.375 ≈ 21°), the wrong second moment in the denominator. About 34° is tan⁻¹(Iyy/Ixy) = tan⁻¹(0.667), the reciprocal of the correct ratio, which gives the complementary angle.

questions.q: Explain why the formula σ = My/I cannot be used for a Z-section stringer bent about its horizontal centroidal axis, and outline how the correct stress distribution is found.
markScheme: Z-section has no axis of symmetry in the loading plane, so Ixy ≠ 0
A moment about x causes curvature about both axes; neutral axis is inclined
Find centroid, then Ixx, Iyy, Ixy (thin-walled approximation, parallel axis theorem)
Use σ = [(My Ixx − Mx Ixy)x + (Mx Iyy − My Ixy)y]/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²)
Neutral axis from σ = 0; peak stresses at points furthest from the neutral axis (may be the flange tips)
questions.modelAnswer: σ = My/I assumes the section is symmetric about the plane of loading, so that the neutral axis is perpendicular to that plane. A Z-section has Ixy ≠ 0 about its horizontal and vertical centroidal axes, so a moment about the x axis produces curvature about both axes and the neutral axis is inclined. To find the stresses: locate the centroid (at the web centre for a Z by point symmetry); compute Ixx, Iyy and Ixy using the thin-walled approximation and parallel axis theorem; then apply σ = [(My Ixx − Mx Ixy)x + (Mx Iyy − My Ixy)y]/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²). The neutral axis comes from setting σ = 0, and the largest stresses occur at the points furthest from it, which may be the corners or the flange tips rather than simply the points with the largest y.

questions.q:
A propped cantilever ABC has a built-in support at A and a simple (prop) support at C. The span AC = 4 m, EI is constant, and the beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 6 kN/m over its full length.
(a) Using superposition of standard cantilever results, find the prop reaction at C. [6]
(b) Find the reaction and the fixing moment at A. [4]
(c) Find the position and magnitude of the maximum sagging bending moment. [5]
(d) Locate the point of contraflexure and sketch the bending moment diagram. [5]
markScheme: (a) Released cantilever tip deflection wL⁴/(8EI) downward; prop force gives RL³/(3EI) upward
(a) Compatibility at C gives R_C = 3wL/8 = 9 kN
(b) Vertical equilibrium R_A = 24 − 9 = 15 kN
(b) Moments about A: M_A = R_C L − wL²/2 = 36 − 48 = −12 kN m (hogging, magnitude wL²/8)
(c) From C: Q = 9 − 6x = 0 at x = 1.5 m
(c) M_max = 9 × 1.5 − 3 × 1.5² = 6.75 kN m sagging (9wL²/128)
(d) M = 9x − 3x² = 0 at x = 3 m from C (1 m from A)
(d) Sketch: parabola, zero at C, +6.75 at 1.5 m, zero at 3 m, −12 at A
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Remove the prop at C to leave a cantilever built in at A. Under w = 6 kN/m the tip deflects down by wL⁴/(8EI). The prop reaction R_C acting upward alone deflects the tip up by R_C L³/(3EI). The real beam has zero deflection at C, so R_C L³/(3EI) = wL⁴/(8EI), giving R_C = 3wL/8 = 3 × 6 × 4/8 = 9 kN.

(b) Total load = wL = 24 kN, so R_A = 24 − 9 = 15 kN (= 5wL/8). Taking moments about A for the whole beam, with sagging positive and the beam to the right of A: M_A = R_C × 4 − 24 × 2 = 36 − 48 = −12 kN m, i.e. a hogging moment of 12 kN m (= wL²/8).

(c) Measure x from C. Q(x) = 9 − 6x and M(x) = 9x − 3x². The maximum sagging moment occurs where Q = 0: x = 1.5 m from C (= 3L/8). M_max = 9 × 1.5 − 3 × 2.25 = 13.5 − 6.75 = 6.75 kN m (= 9wL²/128). Check at A: M(4) = 36 − 48 = −12 kN m, matching part (b).

(d) M = 0 when 9x − 3x² = 0, i.e. x = 0 (at C) or x = 3 m from C, which is 1 m from A. This is the point of contraflexure. The bending moment diagram is a single parabola: zero at C, rising to +6.75 kN m (sagging) at 1.5 m from C, falling through zero at 3 m from C, and reaching −12 kN m (hogging) at A. The shear force diagram is a straight line from +9 kN at C to −15 kN at A, crossing zero at 1.5 m from C.

questions.q:
A thin-walled Z-section stringer has a vertical web of depth 100 mm and two horizontal flanges each 50 mm wide; the top flange projects to the right (+x) from the top of the web and the bottom flange to the left (−x) from the bottom of the web. The wall thickness is 2 mm throughout. Use the thin-walled approximation and centroidal axes with x horizontal and y vertically upwards.
(a) Explain why the centroid lies at the mid-point of the web. [2]
(b) Calculate Ixx, Iyy and Ixy. [8]
(c) The section carries a bending moment Mx = 1 kN m (positive, causing tension where y > 0) and My = 0. Find the direct stress at the web–top-flange corner and at the tip of the top flange. [6]
(d) Find the inclination of the neutral axis and comment on the result compared with simple bending theory. [4]
markScheme: (a) Section has point (rotational) symmetry about web mid-point, so centroid is there
(b) Iyy = 2[t b³/12 + b t (b/2)²] = 1.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴ (web contribution negligible)
(c) σ = Mx(Iyy y − Ixy x)/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²), denominator 4.86 × 10¹⁰ mm⁸
(c) Corner (0, 50): +171 MPa; flange tip (50, 50): −86 MPa
(d) Neutral axis y = (Ixy/Iyy)x, tan α = 1.5, α ≈ 56° to x axis
(d) Comment: σ = My/I would give 75 MPa everywhere along the top flange; Ixy ≠ 0 means bending about both axes and an inclined neutral axis
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Rotating the section by 180° about the mid-point of the web maps it onto itself (the top-right flange becomes the bottom-left flange). So the first moments of area about that point are zero and the centroid lies there.

(b) Take the origin at the centroid. Each flange has area A = 50 × 2 = 100 mm²; the web has area 200 mm².
Ixx: web t h³/12 = 2 × 100³/12 = 1.667 × 10⁵ mm⁴; each flange A ȳ² = 100 × 50² = 2.5 × 10⁵ mm⁴ (its own bt³/12 is negligible). Ixx = 1.667 × 10⁵ + 2 × 2.5 × 10⁵ = 6.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴.
Iyy: each flange t b³/12 + A x̄² = 2 × 50³/12 + 100 × 25² = 2.08 × 10⁴ + 6.25 × 10⁴ = 8.33 × 10⁴ mm⁴; the web lies on x = 0 and contributes only a negligible t³ term. Iyy = 1.67 × 10⁵ mm⁴.
Ixy: each flange's own product term is zero (it is symmetric about its own centroidal axes), so Ixy = Σ A x̄ ȳ = 100 × 25 × 50 + 100 × (−25) × (−50) = 2.50 × 10⁵ mm⁴; the web has x̄ = 0 and contributes nothing.

(c) With My = 0: σ = Mx(Iyy y − Ixy x)/(Ixx Iyy − Ixy²). The denominator is 6.667 × 10⁵ × 1.667 × 10⁵ − (2.5 × 10⁵)² = 1.111 × 10¹¹ − 6.25 × 10¹⁰ = 4.86 × 10¹⁰ mm⁸. With Mx = 10⁶ N mm:
Corner (0, 50): σ = 10⁶ × 1.667 × 10⁵ × 50/4.86 × 10¹⁰ = +171 MPa (tension).
Flange tip (50, 50): σ = 10⁶ × (8.33 × 10⁶ − 12.5 × 10⁶)/4.86 × 10¹⁰ = −86 MPa (compression).

(d) The neutral axis is where σ = 0: Iyy y = Ixy x, so y/x = Ixy/Iyy = 1.5 and the axis is inclined at tan⁻¹1.5 ≈ 56° to the x axis. Simple bending theory would put the neutral axis along x and predict σ = Mx y/Ixx = 75 MPa all along the top flange. The real stress varies from +171 MPa at the corner to −86 MPa at the tip, so simple theory underestimates the peak stress by more than a factor of two and even gets the sign wrong at the tip. Because Ixy ≠ 0, the section bends about both axes and deflects sideways as well as vertically.
